text:
The story going around says a Black island community sold itself the whole island for one dollar and kept it forever. That story is not true, and I need you to hear the real one, because the real one is harder and it is theirs. They did buy their land, in 1871, out of their own pockets, six years after the government promised it and snatched the promise back.

Then they spent a century watching it get traded away acre for acre by a man who owned every job and the only boat.

Three men who had been owned as property on Sapelo Island bought six hundred and fifty acres of it in 1871. Ninety-three years later the last family living on that ground carried its furniture out and moved two miles south.

Their names were William Hillery, John Grovner, and Bilali Bell.

Understand what that signature was. These were men whose own bodies had been listed in somebody's ledger, who had been valued in dollars alongside livestock and rice barrels, and who were now sitting down to be the buyer instead of the merchandise.

The tract cost two thousand dollars. They put five hundred down and carried the rest on a note, which means three men who had owned nothing at all a few years before had somehow saved five hundred dollars and then convinced a white seller to trust them for the balance.

The place was called Raccoon Bluff, on the island's northeast side, up where the land rises and you can see water. It was the only ground on Sapelo that Thomas Spalding, who at his peak held four hundred and twenty-one people in bondage, had never managed to buy.

They cut it into smaller pieces and sold those to other freedmen and their families, at prices those families could reach. Others bought their own tracts the same way, sixty acres at Lumber Landing, fifty at Belle Marsh, and by 1878 families were buying ground at Hog Hammock and Shell Hammock too.

This was not a gift.

Six years earlier the federal government had promised them land and then taken the promise back, and every adult standing on that bluff in 1871 remembered exactly how that had gone.

In January 1865, General Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15. By that August, three hundred and fifty-two freed people were living on Sapelo, and the Freedmen's Bureau had written down seven hundred and forty-five acres issued to twenty-five families, one hundred and seven people in all.

Names on a government list, acreage beside each one, a number for every household.

In September, President Andrew Johnson rescinded the order. The land went back to the men who had held it before, and the families who had been counted were simply uncounted, their names still sitting in a file that no longer meant anything.

The next September, twelve leaders on Sapelo were jailed for refusing to do what the newly appointed Bureau agents told them to do. Several of those agents had money or family tied up in the very plantations they had been sent to supervise.

What Washington would not deed them, they stopped waiting for and went and paid cash for.

On the second of October, 1898, a hurricane came up the Georgia coast and took the church at Hanging Bull with it. The settlement there broke apart and the families scattered to other parts of the island.

When the water pulled back, there was lumber lying on the beach. Boards and timbers the storm had ripped off boats and buildings somewhere and thrown back up onto the sand among the oyster shells.

They walked the tide line and gathered it. They hauled it up to Raccoon Bluff and built a church out of it, finishing around 1900, with a Gothic arch set into each gable.

A house of worship raised out of salvage, out of what the ocean had wrecked and handed back, by people who had been counted as property inside of one lifetime.

Raccoon Bluff grew into the largest Black settlement on the island. One federal census counted a hundred and ninety-four people there in forty-three households, and the island's school for Black children stood on that ground too.

By 1910 there were five hundred and twenty-nine Black people living on Sapelo in a hundred and nine households. There were sixteen white people, in five.

For a moment on that island, in the middle of Jim Crow Georgia, the arithmetic ran the other way.

Two years later a Detroit automobile engineer named Howard Coffin bought the rest of the island for a hundred and fifty thousand dollars. Everything except the Black communities, which were not for sale to him.

Coffin rebuilt Spalding's old tabby mansion on the south end and filled it with famous people. Calvin Coolidge came in 1928, Charles Lindbergh in 1929, Herbert Hoover in 1932.

The crash of 1929 broke him. In 1934 he sold Sapelo to a twenty-nine-year-old tobacco heir named Richard J. Reynolds Jr., who wanted the island as a private retreat and a hunting preserve.

Reynolds's purchase carved out the Black-held ground exactly as Coffin's had. Hog Hammock, Raccoon Bluff, Belle Marsh, Lumber Landing, Shell Hammock, and the burying ground at Behavior were all excluded from the sale.

He wanted them anyway, and unlike the storm and unlike the Freedmen's Bureau, he had time.

Reynolds owned the jobs. He also owned the boat to the mainland, which meant he owned the way off the island, the way back, and the doctor.

In 1949 a man named Hicks Walker was clearing his land at Belle Marsh.

He worked for Reynolds, often up at the mansion on the south end. That house stood on the same footprint as the plantation house where his own daughter's ancestor, an African Muslim named Bilali Muhammad, had been held and made to run the place.

Walker went into that house to work, and came home down the sand roads under the live oaks to his own ground.

He had a wife, Hettie Bryant, and a four-year-old girl born right there at Belle Marsh in 1945. He was clearing the land because he was going to build his house on it.

Reynolds's manager was a white man named Frank Durant, and everybody on Sapelo called him Cap'n Frank. He came down to Belle Marsh one day to see what Walker meant to do with the lumber he was after.

That was the only time he came. After that he simply found Walker wherever Walker happened to be, up on the north end at work, or down on the south end collecting his pay on a Friday.

Move up to Hog Hammock, Hicks. Your uncle Nero has died and you are down there by yourself now, the children walk too far to school, you walk too far to work, and if anybody takes sick you walk too far to get help.

Walker kept clearing his land.

So the offer got better. The sawmill was right there on the island, Cap'n Frank pointed out, and any man who moved to Hog Hammock could have all the lumber he wanted for nothing.

All he would have to pay for were the doors, the windows, and the tin.

That is what a house cost on Sapelo Island in 1949, if you were willing to build it somewhere else. Doors, windows, tin.

Walker kept clearing his land.

So they offered to keep paying his wages the whole time he built the new place, so that moving would not cost him one day's work or one day's pay. A man could put up a house and never miss a check.

Walker kept clearing his land.

Then Cap'n Frank told him it would be a shame if he lost his job and had to go over to the mainland, and left his family down here to fend for themselves.

Every previous offer had been about lumber. This one was about his wife and his little girl, and about the boat, and about who owned it.

His daughter, writing this down half a century later, said what everybody on that island already knew. When a man puts the words job and family in the same breath, that is not a suggestion.

Walker went home that evening and did not curse in front of the white man, because a Black man in coastal Georgia in 1949 did not do that. He got back to Belle Marsh and let it out to Hettie instead, in his own house, in front of his own family, about his own land.

He did not want to move. It was his ground, bought by people who had bought it out of nothing, and he had spent months clearing it with his hands to put a roof on it.

He moved.

The four-year-old grew up to be Cornelia Walker Bailey. Belle Marsh, the settlement she was born in, does not exist.

The arrangement Reynolds offered was an even trade on paper. Give up your acres at Belle Marsh or Raccoon Bluff, take the same number of acres at Hog Hammock, and the house would be built for you and hauled down there free of charge.

Acre for acre, and a free house, and your wages kept whole. Written out like that, it reads almost generous.

A Raccoon Bluff man named Allen Green was asked years afterward why people had left. He said Reynolds wanted everybody together in one settlement so that he could do more for them, and then he said the true thing in five words.

"That was a trap set."

Belle Marsh emptied first, beginning in 1949.

Lumber Landing closed in 1956. Shell Hammock, the settlement closest to the mansion, closed around 1960, and apartments for visiting marine scientists went up on that ground.

Raccoon Bluff held on longest, because Raccoon Bluff was the oldest and the biggest and the one they had bought first. Families there had deeds going back to the Hillery Company, passed down through three generations, and they knew what those deeds had cost.

In 1963 the congregation stopped worshipping in the storm-lumber church and started meeting at Hog Hammock instead. In 1968 they built a new First African Baptist down there, and the old one went quiet.

House by house, the bluff came apart. Some places were jacked up and hauled the two miles south whole, some were taken to pieces and carried down as boards, and some were simply knocked flat and left.

In 1964 a man named George Grovner shut his door at Raccoon Bluff for the last time and walked away from it.

Ninety-three years earlier, a Grovner had helped put five hundred dollars down on that exact ground.

When it was finished, every building at Raccoon Bluff was gone except one. The church stood by itself at the end of a sand road with no community around it, holding boards a hurricane had delivered sixty-four years before.

Reynolds died that same year, 1964. His widow sold the north end of Sapelo to the State of Georgia in 1969 and the south end in 1976.

Nine thousand acres of it became a hunting preserve. The state sells permits there now for deer, small game and feral hog, across ground where four communities once grew their own food.

Researchers who went back through the census schedules and the surveyors' maps estimate the relocations touched at least twenty-seven households and possibly as many as forty-six. About five hundred Geechee people were living on Sapelo in the early 1950s, and Cornelia Bailey put it at about sixty by 2008.

Fewer than fifty live there full time now.

Cornelia Walker Bailey did not let it go. She came back to Sapelo in 1966 and made herself the island's griot, the one who carries the history, and she spent the rest of her life saying out loud what had been done to her father and to everybody else's father.

She wrote about what they ate, because that is where a people's life actually lives. Hominy grits her father cooked as a treat, alligator, wild turkey, gannet, turtle, deer, squirrel, rabbit, raccoon, possum, some of it in season and some of it poached.

"Sometimes nothing at all."

In 2000 she published the whole thing in a book, her father's story included, in plain sentences nobody could argue with. She said their tale had been kept so private that it had never been told before.

Hicks Walker lived on in Hog Hammock, in the house the lumber built, for more than fifty years. A visitor who came to the island in July 2002 was taken to meet him at his residence, an old man in a settlement he had not chosen.

He never did put up a house on the land he cleared at Belle Marsh.

Meanwhile the state was still working. Into the mid-1980s the Department of Natural Resources kept a map on an office wall with a red circle drawn around Hog Hammock, and beside the circle somebody had written that it was to be acquired.

The map came down after a landowner dispute. The intention did not need a map.

In 2012 the county reassessed property on Sapelo and some appraisals jumped by more than a thousand percent overnight. Families who could not find the money lost their ground at delinquent tax auctions before the county rolled most of the values back.

Land held since Reconstruction, sold off the courthouse steps over a tax bill.

Residents sued over paying taxes for services they were not getting, and a 2022 settlement froze island assessments through 2025. Then, on the twelfth of September, 2023, the county commission voted three to two to more than double the size of house allowed in Hogg Hummock, from fourteen hundred square feet to three thousand.

The county's signs say Hog Hammock, and the people who live there say Hogg Hummock and always have, which tells you plainly enough who has been holding the pen.

Bigger houses mean bigger valuations, and bigger valuations mean tax bills that a community of fixed incomes and heirs property cannot carry. They had watched this exact thing happen on Hilton Head and on St. Simons, and they knew what came next.

So they went and got signatures, house by house, across a whole county. It was enough to force a referendum.

The county sued to stop the vote while early ballots were already being cast. It went to the Georgia Supreme Court, which ruled against the county unanimously, and in January 2026 McIntosh County finally voted.

They repealed the rezoning by better than five to one.

The tax question did not leave with it. In December 2025 the county's chief appraiser told the board of assessors that a Sapelo tax bill of roughly eighteen hundred dollars was headed toward about ten thousand, phased in a third at a time.

That is the sum being asked of the great-grandchildren of the people who put five hundred dollars down in 1871.

The state owns about ninety-six percent of the island around them. The county commission is scheduled to vote again this August on what may be built on the rest.

A descendant named Josiah Watts told a reporter in July that three years of this has worn people down. He said the community is not finished with it yet.

"We are still here."

In 2000 the Sapelo Island Cultural and Revitalization Society, the state, and a group of art students went out and restored the church at Raccoon Bluff, which had stood empty by then for thirty-two years.

It is on the National Register now. The roof is sound, the Gothic arches are true, and the boards the ocean threw up in 1898 are still holding.

It sits inside a state hunting preserve, at the end of a short sand road, with nothing around it in any direction. The people who built it are two miles south, arguing about square footage and appraisals.

The building got preserved. The community that built it did not.

There is a National Register listing for that church, and another for the burying ground at Behavior, where Cornelia Bailey was laid in October 2017. There is a road on the state map still called Belle Marsh Road, running past a settlement that is not there.

Not one of those records contains a line about the doors, the windows, and the tin.

Which means somebody outside the record has to be the one to carry it.

The people of Sapelo Island did not inherit their land by accident. They bought it, built on it, worshipped on it, and fought to keep a place their ancestors had once been denied. Their story is more than what was lost. It is a record of what they built.

Starbucks’ move into Xinjiang comes as part of the company’s new Chinese investment and ownership structure: in April of this year, Chinese company Boyu Capital (博裕资本) became 60% owner of Starbucks’ China operations. The promotion of the new stores — particularly the Xinjiang International Grand Bazaar flagship store (the second store is located at Tianshan International Airport) — has also taken a distinctly local approach. Rather than emphasizing the arrival of a foreign brand in a new frontier market, Starbucks has presented itself as a brand adapting to, and becoming part of, its new local surroundings. The brand’s Urumqi debut marks its first expansion into the region since entering the Chinese market over 26 years ago. Back then, Starbucks mostly targeted white-collar workers, focused on first- and second-tier cities, and, for many, symbolized cosmopolitan, urban life.

text:
Depends on whether the cost of the Tabasco network is judged to exceed the cooperation perks still coming from Sheinbaum’s more technocratic side, adjusted for the domestic political return now available from a harder line.

That cooperation currently has a measurable value: migration enforcement that holds southwest border numbers below earlier peaks, a limited set of extraditions, continuity under USMCA that supports nearshoring and manufacturing supply chains, and enough information-sharing for U.S. agencies to act against cartel targets without absorbing the full political cost of intervention. While those outputs hold, treating the broader Morena structure as a difficult but usable partner remains the lower-cost option for the Trump administration. A public demand for regime change before that calculation shifts would risk trade disruption and a migration surge for limited gain.

The offsetting cost is the channel associated with Andrés Manuel “Andy” López Beltrán and the Tabasco group. U.S. agencies have been reviewing accusations linking his circle to organized-crime contacts and large-scale fuel smuggling; no formal investigation has been opened. Separate Mexican investigative accounts and leaked recordings place close associates in fuel-smuggling and extortion activity tied to CJNG cells in Veracruz and Tabasco, including protection arrangements that ran through security officials appointed while Adán Augusto López was governor. 

Those arrangements generate revenue and logistics that support precursor movement and local territorial control. So long as the technocratic wing Sheinbaum represents can still deliver border and extradition results, Washington has treated this as a corruption problem inside a partner government. If the results stop improving, or if a seizure, financial trace, or cluster of U.S. deaths makes the political protection clear and expensive, the cooperation premium no longer covers the cost.

Two additional factors now lower that threshold. First, a visible campaign against the cartels offers the Republican base a concrete demonstration of force after the Iran episode, where the costs were high and the result contested. Action against Mexican narcoterrorism networks is closer to home, easier to explain in terms of fentanyl deaths and border control, and does not require the same extended overseas commitment. That political return for Trump is real and counts in the decision. 

Second, Brazil’s shift to Bolsonaro makes a regional coalition plausible. A Shield of the Americas framing (limited to governments willing to treat narcoterrorism based in Mexico as a shared hemispheric threat) gives Washington partners for intelligence, financial pressure, and political cover without needing a universal Latin American consensus. It does not remove Mexican sovereignty constraints or the risk of trade and migration blowback, but it reduces the isolation cost of acting unilaterally against the cartels.

The steps that follow remain sequential. Sanctions and visa actions against specific operators come first. Pressure on trade rules or ports tied to compromised customs channels can follow. Wider direct action against cartel infrastructure becomes more likely if Mexican forces will not clear it, and easier to present as a regional coalition effort once Brazil is aligned. Open talk of regime change is still a last resort, and only after an assessment that Sheinbaum’s wing is either unable or unwilling to cut the Tabasco channel. 

Until that assessment is reached, the residual cooperation from Sheinbaum still reduces border crossings and keeps supply chains intact. However, the hemisphere’s political shift and the U.S. domestic need for a clearer win after Iran change the price of waiting; but they do not erase the operational limits.

 Senator Flavio Bolsonaro held a narrowing lead in the first round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, after more than half the votes ​were counted, with pollster Datafolha projecting that the election would proceed to a second vote.

Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro who hopes to return his father's right-wing movement to power, was leading leftist President Luiz Inacio ‌Lula da Silva, 80, who is seeking a fourth term, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.

With about 65% of votes reported, Flavio led Lula with 49.58% of the votes to the president's 42.25%. A candidate must pass 50% in order to win outright in the first round.

The two leading candidates were expected to head into a second round vote, Brazilian pollster Datafolha said. Surveys have shown Lula and Flavio polling roughly even in an October 25 runoff.

Early results showed southern states that lean to Bolsonaro reporting faster, while votes from Lula's northeast stronghold are tallied more slowly.

Analysts told Reuters ​they believed Flavio was receiving "protest votes" of people voting against Lula rather than for the right-wing senator - votes they had been expected to save until a second round.

A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America ​by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.

Despite growing worries over Brazil's public finances and ⁠sluggish economic growth, the campaign offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.

UNDECIDED VOTERS
While polls right up until Saturday showed Lula would likely lead the first round but not avoid a runoff, Flavio told journalists in Rio de Janeiro he was ​confident he could win the presidency in the first round, citing voters' frustration with his chief opponent.

OUTSIDE INTERFERENCE
Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted ​Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.

ECONOMIC HEADWINDS
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living ​concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as ​the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief ⁠for families.
Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil's next president will need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to 2.0% and 2.3% respectively.

Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the ​now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of ⁠Brazil's political class and renewed public anger over corruption."

> His team found alternate equipment in Juarez, brought it north and made a midnight push to get the power on.

> Starbucks opened and operated for about 19 months before being selected for closure.

> He learned about it through an outside firm calling to negotiate a lease termination.

> He says the initial offer was roughly 2–3% of the remaining lease value.

We all have the choice of how we behave and how we treat other people. Please do better.

text:
Here's the hundred-year arc, era by era. 

A few terms first, 
since they come up constantly:

Zionism –
the political movement (from the 1880s–90s) to build a Jewish homeland in the historic Land of Israel, which was then "Palestine," a backwater province of the Ottoman (Turkish) Empire.

Aliyah ("going up") –
 Jewish immigration to the Land.
 Historians number the waves:
 First Aliyah, Second, etc.

Yishuv – the Jewish community living
 in Palestine before 1948.

Pogrom – 
an organized mob attack on Jews, 
mostly in the Russian Empire.

Mandate – 
after WWI the League of Nations gave 
Britain legal authority to 
govern Palestine (1920–48).

Dunam – 
the local land unit, 
about a quarter acre.

1850–1880: Groundwork, 
before Zionism existed

Setting: 
Palestine has roughly 400,000 people, mostly Arab Muslims; about 10,000–25,000 Jews (the "Old Yishuv"), religious, living on charity in Jerusalem, Safed, Tiberias and Hebron.

Sir Moses Montefiore 
(British financier, Rothschild's brother-in-law) – 
1860 builds Mishkenot Sha'ananim, the first Jewish neighborhood outside Jerusalem's walls, using money left by Judah Touro (New Orleans merchant). → Proved Western Jewish money could create facts on the ground.

Alliance Israélite Universelle (
Paris, 1860) and Charles Netter –
1870 open Mikveh Israel, an agricultural school near Jaffa. → Jews had been barred from farmland in Europe for centuries; the whole project needed Jewish farmers.

Moses Hess 
(1862, Rome and Jerusalem) –
 first modern argument that Jews are a nation that should return on its own, not wait for a Messiah.

Petah Tikva (1878) – first modern Jewish farm colony, founded by Jerusalem Jews (Yehoshua Stampfer, Yoel Moshe Salomon). Malaria wiped it out; revived in 1883 with Rothschild money. → The template, and the warning, for every colony after.

============================

1881–1903: 
First Aliyah – pogroms, Rothschild, Herzl

1881: 
Tsar Alexander II is assassinated; pogroms sweep Russia; 1882 "May Laws" squeeze Jews out of villages. About 2 million Jews flee by 1914, the vast majority to America. Only ~25,000–35,000 go to Palestine = the First Aliyah. → The push factor. America was Plan A; Palestine was Plan B.

Leon Pinsker 
(Odessa doctor), Auto-Emancipation (1882): 
Jews will never be safe without their own land. His Hovevei Zion ("Lovers of Zion") and the student group BILU found Rishon LeZion (1882, led by Zalman David Levontin), Zikhron Ya'akov, Rosh Pinna, Gedera.

Baron Edmond de Rothschild 
(Paris branch of the banking dynasty) – 
from 1883 bankrolls the failing colonies: 
buys land, drains swamps, pays doctors and teachers, builds Carmel Winery (Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov, still Israel's largest). By some estimates over $50 million of that era's money. → Without him the First Aliyah collapses. In 1900 he hands management to the Jewish Colonization Association (founded by railway magnate Baron Maurice de Hirsch); his son James later runs it as PICA.

Eliezer Ben-Yehuda – 
arrives 1881, revives Hebrew as a spoken language (first modern dictionary, newspapers). → One language for Jews arriving from 50 countries.

Theodor Herzl 
(Vienna journalist) – 
covers the 1894 Dreyfus Affair (a French Jewish officer framed for treason) and concludes assimilation has failed. 1896 publishes Der Judenstaat; 1897 convenes the First Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland, creating the World Zionist Organization (WZO). 

Writes in his diary that at Basel he founded 
the Jewish state and that in fifty years 
everyone would see it. 

Fifty years later: 1947. 
→ Turned a scattered idea into an international political body with a congress, a bank and a diplomatic strategy. Died 1904 at 44.

Jewish Colonial Trust 
(London, 1899) – the WZO's bank.
Its subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company, opens in Jaffa in 1903 under Levontin. → Credit for land purchases; by 1948 it was the de facto central bank and printed Israel's first banknotes. Today it's Bank Leumi.

Jewish National Fund (JNF/KKL, 1901) –
 buys land as the permanent property of the Jewish people (never resold, leased only to Jewish settlers). Funded by blue tin collection boxes in Jewish homes worldwide; run by Menachem Ussishkin 1923–41. → By 1947 Jews owned ~7% of Palestine, about half of it JNF land, and those blocks shaped where the 1947 partition line could be drawn.

1903 Kishinev pogrom (49 dead).
 Britain offers Herzl territory in East Africa ("the Uganda plan"); Russian Zionists reject it. → Settled that only Palestine would do.

1904–1914: 
Second Aliyah –
 the socialists who built the state's skeleton

~35,000 young Russian Jewish socialists arrive after the failed 1905 revolution. Among them David Ben-Gurion (born David Grün, arrives 1906), Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, Berl Katznelson, A.D. Gordon, Levi Eshkol. Creed: Jews must do their own physical labor ("Hebrew labor"). → These men ran the country for the next forty years.

Arthur Ruppin (German sociologist) –
 1908 opens the WZO's Palestine Office in Jaffa and founds the Palestine Land Development Company to buy, drain and parcel land. → "Father of Zionist settlement": charity colonies become a planned national program.

Yehoshua Hankin –
 the chief land buyer, ~600,000 dunams over his life, including the Jezreel Valley from the Sursock family, absentee landlords in Beirut (1920s). → Created the contiguous blocks that became the state; also displaced Arab tenant farmers, an early seed of the conflict.

Tel Aviv (1909) –
 66 families draw seashells for lots in the dunes north of Jaffa; Meir Dizengoff becomes first mayor. → The Yishuv's economic capital, and where independence was declared.

Degania (1909–10) –
 the first kibbutz (communal farm), on the Sea of Galilee. → Kibbutzim became the frontier posts that fixed borders and supplied the army's elite units.

HaShomer ("The Watchman," 1909, Israel and Manya Shochat) – Jewish armed guards replacing hired guards. → Ancestor of the Haganah, which became the army.
Technion (Haifa, founded 1912, opened 1924) – funded by the Wissotzky Tea fortune (Moscow) and New York banker Jacob Schiff. → Engineers.

Aaron Aaronsohn – botanist who discovered wild emmer wheat; his Atlit research station is funded by Julius Rosenwald of Sears, Roebuck. (He matters again in a minute.)

By 1914 the Yishuv is roughly 85,000 Jews in 40+ settlements.

1914–1918: 
World War I – the Balfour Declaration

The Ottomans join Germany.
The Yishuv suffers famine, locusts and deportations (Jaffa and Tel Aviv emptied in 1917); the population falls to ~56,000.

NILI spy ring 
(Aaronsohn, his sister Sarah Aaronsohn, Avshalom Feinberg) – passes Turkish positions to British intelligence; Sarah is captured, tortured, and shoots herself in 1917. → Goodwill with the British just as they took Palestine.

Zion Mule Corps
 (Gallipoli 1915, Joseph Trumpeldor) and the Jewish Legion (1917–18, lobbied into existence by Ze'ev Jabotinsky; Ben-Gurion and Ben-Zvi enlist). → First Jewish military units in 1,800 years; the Haganah's founding cadre.

Chaim Weizmann –
 Russian-born chemist at Manchester University. In 1915–16 he invents a fermentation process to mass-produce acetone, which Britain needs for cordite (artillery explosive). 

This puts him in the rooms of Lloyd George and Balfour. → Access to Britain's leaders at the exact moment Britain was conquering Palestine. Later Israel's first president.

2 Nov 1917, Balfour Declaration – Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour's letter to Lord Walter Rothschild (London branch of the family, a leader of British Jewry): Britain "views with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people." 

→ The first great-power promise, later written into the League of Nations Mandate, making it international law. (Britain had also made overlapping promises to the Arabs and to France.)

Dec 1917 General Allenby takes Jerusalem; 
by late 1918 all of Palestine

1920–1929: 
The Mandate – a "state within a state"

1920 San Remo conference gives Britain the Palestine Mandate; the League of Nations confirms it in 1922 with the Balfour wording built in, plus a "Jewish Agency" to work with the government. 

Sir Herbert Samuel, 
a British Jew, is the first High Commissioner (1920–25). In 1922 Britain carves off Transjordan (the east bank) from the national-home provisions.

Violence: 
Tel Hai (1920, Trumpeldor killed), Jerusalem riots (1920), Jaffa riots (1921, 47 Jews killed). → The Haganah ("Defense") is founded in June 1920 as an underground militia.

Histadrut 
(General Federation 
of Hebrew Workers, Dec 1920;

 Ben-Gurion as secretary-general 1921–35). 
Not just a union; it owned companies: Solel Boneh (construction, 1921: roads, housing, later British army bases), Bank Hapoalim (1921, "Workers' Bank," now one of Israel's two biggest), Tnuva (dairy and farm co-op, 1926), 

Hamashbir (consumer co-op), 
Kupat Holim (health fund). It also controlled the Haganah. → By 1948 the Yishuv already had an economy, a health system, a labor force and an army under one leadership. Declaring a state was mostly changing the letterhead.

Keren Hayesod 
("Foundation Fund," 1920) –
 the WZO's main fundraising arm for immigration and settlement. The Jewish Agency for Palestine (1929) brings in wealthy non-Zionist Americans like Louis Marshall and banker Felix Warburg (Kuhn, Loeb). → The recognized "government in waiting"; Ben-Gurion chairs it 1935–48.

Pinhas Rutenberg 
(Russian-Jewish engineer, former revolutionary) – wins the 1921 electricity concession; Palestine Electric Company (1923, chaired by Lord Reading, Rufus Isaacs, a British Jew who had been Viceroy of India); Naharayim hydro plant on the Jordan (1932). → Electrified the country and made industry possible. Today the Israel Electric Corporation.

Industry:
 Michael Pollak founds Nesher cement (1923); Shemen oil and soap in Haifa (1920s). → Local building materials and consumer goods that mattered when the country was blockaded in 1948.

Third Aliyah
 (1919–23, ~35,000 pioneers) and Fourth Aliyah (1924–29, ~80,000, mostly Polish middle class). The US Immigration Act of 1924 slams America's door, so Jews who would have gone to New York go to Tel Aviv. → Numbers.
Hebrew University opens on Mount Scopus in 1925 (Balfour attends; Einstein and Weizmann on the board).

1929: 
Western Wall riots and the Hebron massacre (67 Jews killed; 133 Jews and 116 Arabs dead overall). → The Haganah professionalizes; in 1931 the right-wing Irgun (Jabotinsky's movement) splits off. Britain's 1930 Passfield White Paper tries to curb immigration and is reversed in 1931 after Zionist lobbying.

1930–1939: Hitler, the Arab Revolt, the first partition plan

Moshe Novomeysky (Siberian mining engineer) – 1930 Dead Sea potash concession, Palestine Potash Company, plants at Kalia and Sodom; a major supplier of Britain's potash in WWII. → The Yishuv's biggest industrial export. Today Dead Sea Works/ICL.

1933 Hitler takes power. Fifth Aliyah (1929–39, ~250,000 people, including ~60,000 German Jews: doctors, lawyers, architects, hence Tel Aviv's Bauhaus "White City"). 

The Ha'avara (Transfer) Agreement (1933) between the Jewish Agency and Nazi Germany lets emigrating German Jews move part of their wealth out as German export goods. → Bitterly controversial, but it brought tens of millions of dollars in capital and machinery. The Yishuv goes from 175,000 (1931) to ~450,000 (1939).

Diamond cutting starts in Netanya 
(1937, Oved Ben-Ami) with refugees from Antwerp and Amsterdam; by the mid-1940s diamonds are Palestine's largest export. → Hard currency.

Mekorot (national water company, 1937; 
Levi Eshkol, engineer Simcha Blass). Its Negev pipeline lets the Yishuv plant eleven settlements in a single night (Oct 1946). → Water decided where you could settle, and settlement decided where the border went: the Negev stayed inside the Jewish state in the 1947 plan.

1936–39 Arab Revolt – 
general strike and attacks led by the Grand Mufti Haj Amin al-Husseini. Britain crushes it with help from thousands of legally armed Jewish auxiliary police and Orde Wingate's Special Night Squads (a British officer and devout Christian who trained Moshe Dayan and Yigal Allon). 

Meanwhile "Tower and Stockade": 
about 50 settlements built overnight to seize strategic ground. → Two consequences for 1948: the Haganah got training and arms, while the Palestinian Arab leadership was killed, jailed or exiled and disarmed. They entered 1948 with no army.

1937 Peel Commission – 
first official partition proposal 
(Jewish state roughly a fifth of the land). 
Zionists accept the principle; 
Arabs reject it. 

→ The template for 1947.

1939 White Paper – 
Britain caps Jewish immigration at 75,000 over five years, restricts land purchase, and promises an Arab-majority state in ten years, as Hitler's war begins. → Zionists conclude Britain has to be pushed out. Mossad LeAliyah Bet (1938, Shaul Avigur) starts smuggling Jews in illegally.

1939–1945: 
World War II and the Holocaust

Ben-Gurion: 
fight the war as if there were no White Paper, and the White Paper as if there were no war. ~30,000 Palestinian Jews join British forces; the Jewish Brigade fights in Italy in 1945. 

→ Its veterans then run the survivor escape routes 
(Bricha) and arms smuggling across Europe.

Palmach (1941) –
 the Haganah's full-time strike force, set up with British backing when Rommel threatened Egypt; commanders Yitzhak Sadeh, Yigal Allon, Moshe Dayan, Yitzhak Rabin. → The trained core of the 1948 army.

The Holocaust: 
~6 million murdered. 1942 Biltmore Program (New York): Zionism openly demands a Jewish state; the movement's center of gravity shifts from London to Washington, and American Jewry (Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver, Stephen Wise) becomes the decisive lobby.

War economy: 
Solel Boneh builds Allied bases across the Middle East; workshops supply the British army; the Haganah's secret arms industry (Ta'as) and the Ayalon Institute (1945–48), a bullet factory hidden under a kibbutz laundry in Rehovot, turn out over 2 million rounds. → The ammunition and industrial base for 1948.

1944: 
the Irgun under Menachem Begin declares revolt against Britain; the smaller Lehi kills Lord Moyne in Cairo.

1945–1947: 
Pushing Britain out and winning the UN vote

~250,000 Holocaust survivors sit in displaced-persons camps; Britain keeps the White Paper. Truman asks Britain (1945) to admit 100,000; a joint Anglo-American committee agrees (1946); Prime Minister Attlee and Foreign Secretary Bevin refuse. → A US–UK split the Zionists exploit.

1 July 1945, New York: 
Ben-Gurion meets 17 wealthy American Jews at the apartment of Rudolf Sonneborn (chemicals and oil). The "Sonneborn Institute" secretly buys and ships arms-making machinery, ships and aircraft to the Haganah, in violation of US law. → Private American money armed the state before it existed.

Oct 1945–Jul 1946 
the Haganah, Irgun and Lehi coordinate attacks on British infrastructure. Britain's "Black Sabbath" (29 June 1946) arrests the Jewish Agency leadership. 22 July 1946 the Irgun bombs the King David Hotel (British HQ), 91 dead; the Haganah breaks with the Irgun. → Palestine becomes a drain a bankrupt postwar Britain can't afford: 100,000 troops tied down.

Aliyah Bet: 
~66 ships carry ~70,000 survivors toward Palestine (1945–48); Britain intercepts most and interns them on Cyprus. The Exodus 1947 (an old Chesapeake Bay steamer bought with American money and crewed by American volunteers, 4,500 survivors aboard) is rammed by the Royal Navy and its passengers shipped back to Germany in front of UN observers. → The public-relations disaster that turned world opinion.

Feb 1947 Britain hands the problem to the UN. UNSCOP (an 11-country committee) tours Palestine, witnesses the Exodus affair, and a majority recommends partition. → A neutral body endorsed a Jewish state.

29 Nov 1947, UN General Assembly Resolution 181 – partition: a Jewish state on ~55% of the land (including the Negev desert), an Arab state on the rest, Jerusalem under UN control; vote 33–13–10. Both the USA (Truman) and the USSR (Gromyko) vote yes, Moscow because it wanted Britain out of the Middle East. The Jewish Agency accepts; the Arab League and the Palestinian leadership reject it. → The legal birth certificate.

The lobbying: 
Weizmann meets Truman (Nov 1947) and keeps the Negev inside the plan. In March 1948, with the State Department backing away from partition, Eddie Jacobson, Truman's old partner in a Kansas City haberdashery, talks Truman into seeing Weizmann again. → A business friendship kept US support alive.

Dec 1947–May 1948: 
Civil war, and the money and guns

Fighting starts the day after the vote. Palestinian irregulars and the Arab Liberation Army (Fawzi al-Qawuqji) besiege Jerusalem's 100,000 Jews and ambush convoys.

Golda Meir (later prime minister) – 
Jan–Mar 1948 tour of the US raises ~$50 million from American Jews. Ben-Gurion later said history would record that a Jewish woman got the money that made the state possible. → It paid for everything below.

Czech arms deal 
(Jan 1948, negotiated by Ehud Avriel, 

Soviet-approved): 
rifles, machine guns, millions of rounds, 25 Avia S-199 fighters. First shipment lands 1 April 1948. → The Haganah had been critically short of weapons; the fighters stopped an Egyptian column 30 km from Tel Aviv on 29 May.

Al Schwimmer (TWA flight engineer) –
buys surplus US transport planes and three B-17 bombers, smuggles them out through Panama and Czechoslovakia in defiance of the US arms embargo (convicted 1950, pardoned by Clinton in 2001). Later founds Israel Aircraft Industries. → His planes flew the Czech weapons in (Operation Balak).

Yehuda Arazi and Teddy Kollek
 (later Jerusalem's mayor) run Haganah procurement in New York. ~4,000 overseas volunteers (Machal) arrive, including WWII pilots and Col. David "Mickey" Marcus (US Army, West Point), who builds the "Burma Road" bypass that lifts the Jerusalem siege; he's killed by his own sentry in June.

April 1948, Plan Dalet: 
the Haganah goes on the offensive. Tiberias, Haifa, Safed and Jaffa fall; Deir Yassin (9 April, Irgun/Lehi kill ~100 Arab villagers) and the Hadassah medical convoy (13 April, 78 Jewish doctors and nurses killed). Arab flight begins. → The Jewish state had defensible territory before the British left.

May 1948–1949:
Independence and the war

Friday 14 May 1948, 4 pm, Tel Aviv Museum (Dizengoff's old house on Rothschild Boulevard): Ben-Gurion reads the Declaration of Independence. The Mandate ends at midnight; Truman recognizes Israel eleven minutes later; the USSR follows on 17 May.

15 May: 
Egypt, Transjordan (the British-officered Arab Legion under Glubb Pasha), Syria, Lebanon and Iraq invade. The Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem's Old City falls on 28 May.

26 May the Israel Defense Forces are created from the Haganah and Palmach; in June Ben-Gurion sinks the Irgun arms ship Altalena to enforce one army under one government.

Truces in June–July are used to absorb the Czech arms and new immigrants. The "Ten Days" offensive (July) takes Lydda and Ramle (~50,000 Arabs expelled); autumn offensives take the Negev and Galilee; fighting ends in January 1949.

1949 armistice agreements at Rhodes: Egypt (24 Feb), Lebanon (23 Mar), Jordan (3 Apr), Syria (20 Jul). Israel holds ~78% of Mandate Palestine (the plan had given it 55%); Jordan holds the West Bank and East Jerusalem; Egypt holds Gaza. The ceasefire line becomes the "Green Line."

Cost: 
~6,000 Israelis dead, 1% of a population of 650,000. 
About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs become refugees.

Jan 1949 first elections: 
Ben-Gurion prime minister, Weizmann president. 
11 May 1949 Israel joins the UN.

1948–51 the population doubles with
 ~700,000 immigrants: 
European survivors, then Jews from Arab countries. 

Operation Magic Carpet flies
~49,000 Yemenite Jews out on chartered Alaska Airlines planes (1949–50); Ezra and Nehemiah brings ~120,000 from Iraq (1950–51). Zim shipping (1945, Jewish Agency + Histadrut) and El Al (1948) carry them.

5 July 1950, Law of Return – 
any Jew anywhere may immigrate and become a citizen. The March 1950 Absentee Property Law 
transfers refugees' land to the state.

What survived from that century: 
Carmel Winery, Bank Leumi, Bank Hapoalim, the JNF, Israel Electric, Dead Sea Works (ICL), Solel Boneh (now Shikun & Binui), Tnuva, Mekorot, Zim, El Al, Israel Aircraft Industries, Nesher, the Technion and Hebrew University are all still running. 

The recurring pattern: 
a philanthropist or company buys land or builds infrastructure, settlements follow, the settlements fix where the border ends up.

One thing to hold alongside this: the same hundred years look very different from the Palestinian Arab side, where a majority population never consented to the Mandate or partition and 1948 is the Nakba ("catastrophe"). 

Whether this was a people reclaiming an ancient homeland or a settler movement taking a country from its inhabitants is the core of the dispute to this day, and serious historians argue every stage of it. I can go deeper on any single thread here, like the money trail, the land purchases, or the 1948 arms deals.

text:
Acts 15:29 is the closing instruction in a letter from the apostles and elders in Jerusalem to Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia. In the NIV it reads: “You are to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals and from sexual immorality. You will do well to avoid these things. Farewell.”The verse comes from the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), held around AD 49–50. Some Jewish Christians had insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law in order to be saved. The council rejected that requirement. Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and James argued that God had already accepted the Gentiles by faith and given them the Holy Spirit, so salvation is by grace, not by observing the law (Acts 15:7–11, 19). The letter therefore states that the council will not lay any further burden on the Gentiles beyond these four things (Acts 15:28–29).The four abstentions are:Food sacrificed to idols — meat or meals linked to pagan temple worship, which Jewish believers found deeply offensive and which risked association with idolatry.
Blood — a long-standing prohibition rooted in the idea that life is in the blood (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10–14).
Meat of strangled animals — animals not properly drained of blood, so this overlaps with the blood prohibition.
Sexual immorality (Greek porneia) — a broad term covering illicit sexual behavior, especially common in some pagan cults.

These points closely parallel the rules given in Leviticus 17–18 for foreigners living among Israel. In the early church they functioned mainly as practical boundaries that allowed Jewish and Gentile Christians to share table fellowship and worship without constant offense, while distinguishing believers from surrounding pagan practices. The letter presents them as necessary for the sake of unity and holiness in that setting, not as additional conditions for being saved.Later New Testament discussion (especially 1 Corinthians 8–10) treats food offered to idols more as a matter of conscience and concern for weaker believers than as an absolute permanent dietary law, while sexual immorality remains a clear moral prohibition. The council’s core decision stands: Gentiles are full members of the church through faith in Christ alone, without circumcision or the full yoke of the Mosaic law.

Here's a math lesson your local store owner already knows by heart.

The average retailer in America keeps somewhere between 2 and 5 cents of profit on every dollar you spend. That's after rent, payroll, inventory, insurance, utilities, theft, and the long hours nobody sees.

Now look at the receipt. State and local sales taxes typically add 6 to 9 cents on that same dollar.

Think about that. The government didn't stock a single shelf. It didn't sign the lease, make payroll, or stay late to count the register. Yet it walks away with a bigger cut of the sale than the person who did all of it.

Gasoline is the same story, only worse.

The station owner on the corner often clears just pennies per gallon. Meanwhile, the government takes a far bigger bite. The federal tax alone is 18.4 cents a gallon. In California, the state excise tax just climbed to 63.4 cents, and once fees and sales taxes are added, more than $1.20 of every gallon goes to the state.

So when politicians stand at a podium and blame "greedy" businesses for high prices, ask who's actually taking the largest share.

It's like having the mob as your business partner. You put up the money, take the risk, and do all the work. Then your "partner" shows up, contributes nothing, and demands a cut bigger than your own.

The difference is the mob at least pretends to offer protection.

And here's the part that should make everyone angry. Sales taxes are a percentage, so every time prices rise, the government's take rises right along with them. The same people screaming about "price gouging" are quietly cashing in on it.

Your store owner is not the villain here. He's the one getting squeezed from both sides.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Wednesday, October 4, 1967, Braniff International petitioned the Civil Aeronautics Board for nonstop service between Miami, Florida, and London, England. The new route application was announced by Thomas P. “Tom" Robertson, Braniff's Vice President of Regulatory Proceedings. Braniff's latest application joined the Airline’s 17 pending applications for additional routes that were critical to its long-term growth.

If the new route were awarded to Braniff, it would enable the Dallas-based luxury carrier not only to provide service to passengers between London and Miami, but it would also open single-airline service between Europe and Latin America. At the time of the application, Braniff served 13 major cities in South America from Miami.

Boeing 707-327C or Douglas DC-8-62 Intercontinental Jets were initially planned for the two weekly roundtrips and three during peak travel season. After 1970, Braniff intended to operate the proposed Boeing 2707 and Concorde Supersonic Transports over the 4400-mile nonstop flight. However, Concorde service would have required a fueling stop at Washington Dulles Airport. In 1967, Concorde was planned with a range that would not allow a nonstop flight of this length.

Vice President Robertson indicated that the London/Miami route had already been approved by the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom. The two countries had been negotiating and jointly approved that the route could begin on or after January 1, 1970. This authorization was a result of a new US-United Kingdom bi-lateral treaty. However, the new treaty would not and did not indicate what airlines would fly the route. Instead, this decision would be decided by the CAB for the US airlines that had entered applications of the new route.

Mr. Robertson, who commuted every weekend from Washington Dulles to Dallas Love Field, had been with Braniff for 22-years and was highly experienced in navigating the complex issues of a CAB route case. He stated that the airlines involved in the new case would have the opportunity to present their case and rebuttals. Once that was completed, then the CAB Examiner's final report was handed to the CAB Board, which would either deny or approve the Examiner's recommendations. If it was approved, the route was awarded and service began, but if not then the proceedings and rebuttals began again.

The 1967 Miami/London award was given to Miami-based National Airlines. On July 13, 1979, Braniff International filed a petition with the Civil Aeronautics Board asking for authority to provide nonstop Boeing 747 service between Miami International Airport and London Gatwick Airport. Braniff planned to offer several Boeing 747 flights each week between Florida and Great Britain. However, the route was ultimately awarded to Miami-based Air Florida, Inc., which initially operated the route with Douglas DC-8-62 aircraft. Air Florida's DC-8 was Braniff's former famed Calder Flying Colors of South America flying artwork registered as N1805.

What Claude has to say about this post. It's a scam, or at best a bait-and-switch. The "comment CLAUDE, like, retweet, follow" part gives it away. That's engagement farming: the account grows, and whatever arrives in your DMs is usually one of three things:

A paid course or Telegram group dressed up as "free."
A bot that asks for your wallet's private key or seed phrase. It drains the wallet. Fake "Polymarket trading bot" repos on GitHub have been a known way to steal crypto. This is the real danger, not losing $90.
Referral links, where they earn a cut when you sign up and deposit.
Why the $143K claim proves nothing

Every Polymarket wallet is public. Out of thousands, some will be up big, partly by luck. Picking a winner after the fact is easy. Copying it doesn't give you whatever made it win.
The big winning wallets usually have an edge you can't copy from their code. They might be professional market makers, have faster servers, or know something before the market does.
"$90 overnight" is one roll of the dice. It tells you nothing about whether a strategy works.
What are the odds I could build one that works?

Building a bot that trades: easy. I could have one running in an afternoon.
Building one that makes money over time: low odds. Prediction markets are basically zero-sum. Every dollar you win, someone else loses, and fees come off the top. The ways bots do make money (posting buy and sell offers to earn the spread, or exploiting small price gaps between related markets) are crowded with full-time pros on faster setups. Gaps that are easy to find get closed within days.
Something like $143K: very unlikely. The hard part isn't the code. It's having an edge, meaning you know something the market doesn't, or you're faster. A smarter AI doesn't solve that, because everyone else has the same AI.
Where real edges come from is deep knowledge of a specific area, and you happen to have unusual insight into Texas voter turnout. That's a general observation, not a recommendation. I'm not a licensed financial advisor, and I can't tell you whether to put money in.

If you do get the "free" bot from this guy, I can read through its code before you run it and tell you whether it tries to grab your keys or send money anywhere. Want me to do that?

That what I thought... investment banks pay big money to get data ms faster than their competitors trying to arbitrage trades with programed trading

That's the same game. High-frequency trading firms have spent hundreds of millions to shave milliseconds:

Spread Networks spent about $300 million on a fiber line from Chicago to New Jersey, drilled as straight as possible through mountains. It cut the round trip from about 17 milliseconds to about 13.
A few years later, firms switched to microwave towers, because signals travel faster through air than through glass. That made the fiber line second-best almost overnight.
Firms also pay to put their servers in the same building as the exchange ("co-location"), and fight over rack spots closer to the exchange's machines.
So when someone says a laptop and an hour a day will beat the market, they're claiming to beat people who drill through mountains for 4 milliseconds. Polymarket isn't Wall Street, but its bot traders work the same way. The easy money goes to whoever is fastest or best informed, and that's not someone who downloaded a free repo from an X post.

The one area where an individual can sometimes compete is knowledge rather than speed. Speed is a contest of who spends the most money. Knowing a niche better than anyone else isn't.

The new route would have added 789 miles to its route system, which would offer both express and local services.

Braniff express flights would make an intermediate stop at Detroit, Michigan on its way to New York, without any additional stops. However, local schedules would feature multiple stops along the route at Michigan City, Elkhart, and Adrian on the way to Detroit. From Detroit to New York, Braniff flights would stop at Erie, Jamestown, Elmira, Binghamton/Endicott/Johnson City and Wilkes Barre/Scranton and then to Newark and New York.

In addition, during October 1943, Braniff also submitted several route applications that would have enabled the carrier to operate Coast to Coast. Service from Los Angeles to New York and Los Angeles to Atlanta would have been possible on a Braniff airliner, if its petitions were approved by the CAB. The Airline also asked for additional north and south service to further strengthen its dominant position in the Midwest United States, including service at Topeka, Kansas and Moline/Davenport, Illinois/Iowa.

Ultimately, Braniff was not awarded its hoped for transcontinental routes, which would later severely hinder the company and its ability to compete in a deregulated environment beginning in October 1978. It was not until 1979, that Braniff was able to offer coast to coast service. However, service was authorized some years at at Topeka and Moline/Davenport and most importantly a 7719 mile route from the US Mainland to Mexico, Cuba, Centra and South America was awarded in May 1946, making Braniff an international airline for the first time.

Robot Lawn Mower Industry Growth: 2026 Market Data, Adoption Gaps, and a Growth Playbook for Executives 

Robot lawn mower industry growth is the shift of residential and commercial mowing from gas and push equipment to autonomous, battery-powered robots — a category now growing several times faster than the overall lawn mower market. Analysts value the global robotic mower segment somewhere between $1.7 billion and $10.5 billion for 2025, with forecast growth rates of 7.5% to 22% a year. The spread in those numbers is itself the story: this is an early, fast-moving market where the winners will be decided by navigation technology, channel strategy, and how quickly brands crack North America.

This guide is written for executives at robot mower manufacturers, distributors, dealers, and commercial lawn care operators. It consolidates the most-cited public data as of October 2026, explains why the forecasts disagree, and lays out a practical framework for capturing share.

Key Takeaways

The market is real but poorly measured. 2025 size estimates range from $1.71B to $10.50B depending on the research firm. Build your plan on unit and penetration data, not headline dollar figures.

Wire-free is now the default. Wire-free models reportedly rose from 35% to 65% of global robotic mower sales between 2024 and the first half of 2025.

North America is the largest untapped prize. The region drives roughly 60% of global lawn mower sales, yet robotic penetration is estimated in the low single digits — versus roughly 20% in Europe and about 40% in the Nordics.

Margins favor robotics. Robotics-heavy brands have reported gross margins around 50%, well above the roughly 30% typical of traditional outdoor power equipment.

Service, not specs, is the next battleground. As hardware commoditizes, installation, after-sales support, and commercial fleet models will separate leaders from the pack.

How Big Is the Robot Lawn Mower Market? (And Why Nobody Agrees)

Ask five research firms how large the robotic mower market is and you will get five very different answers. That is not a sign the category is overhyped. It is a sign the category is young, fragmented across channels, and changing faster than annual research cycles.

Here is how the most frequently cited public estimates compare.

Why the Estimates Diverge

Three definitional choices explain most of the gap. Executives should check each one before quoting any market figure in a board deck or investor memo.

Scope of “robotic.” Some firms count only fully autonomous consumer units. Others fold in semi-autonomous, commercial ride-on conversions, and accessories.

Revenue basis. Manufacturer shipment value and retail sell-through value can differ by 30–50% once distributor and retail margins are included.

Channel visibility. Direct-to-consumer and marketplace sales from newer Chinese brands are hard to capture in traditional dealer-based surveys, so legacy methodologies tend to undercount them.

The practical takeaway: treat any single dollar figure as directional. Unit volume, penetration rate, and average selling price (ASP) are more reliable building blocks for planning.

Robotic Lawn Mower: Mower Growth by the Numbers

Strip away the dollar estimates and the volume data tells a sharper story. The core distinction executives need to track is lawn mower mower growth overall (slow, roughly 6% a year) versus robotic unit growth (explosive, and concentrated in wire-free models).

Unit Volume Is Accelerating

2.34 million units in H1 2025. Industry data reported by EqualOcean put global smart robotic mower sales at 2.34 million units in the first half of 2025, a 327% year-over-year jump.

Wire-free took over. Wire-free models accounted for about 1.52 million of those units, lifting their share from 35% in 2024 to 65%.

China’s export engine. Chinese lawn mower exports reached roughly RMB 13.2 billion (about $1.9 billion) from January through July 2025, up 56.6% year over year, according to the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, via KrASIA.

Brand-level scale. Segway Navimow announced its one-millionth cumulative unit in April 2026, five years after launching its first wire-free model, and now sells in more than 40 countries.

A note of caution: triple-digit growth rates partly reflect a low base and a seasonal pull-forward of inventory. Expect growth to normalize as the category matures, even as absolute volumes keep climbing.

The Penetration Gap: Where the Growth Will Come From

Penetration — the share of lawn-owning households using a robotic mower — is the single most important metric in this industry. It shows how far each region is from saturation.

The contrast is striking. North America accounts for nearly 60% of global lawn mower sales and has roughly 100 million residential lawns, yet robotic penetration sits in the low single digits. Europe, which spent two decades on boundary-wire products, is already at about one in five households.

Even modest movement in North America would reshape the global market. Every single percentage point of U.S. household penetration represents roughly one million robotic mowers in service.

The Five Forces Driving Robot Lawn Mower Industry Growth

1. The Navigation Leap: From Boundary Wire to RTK, Vision, and LiDAR

Boundary wire was the industry’s biggest adoption barrier. It required professional installation, broke under aeration and digging, and could not adapt to changing landscapes.

Wire-free navigation removed that friction. Today’s leading platforms combine RTK satellite positioning with cameras, LiDAR, or both, enabling virtual boundaries drawn in an app and systematic striped mowing.

Wire-free, multi-sensor platforms like the Mammotion LUBA 3 AWD represent the navigation shift that took wire-free models from roughly a third to nearly two-thirds of the market.

Incumbents have moved decisively. Husqvarna — which launched the world’s first robotic mower 30 years ago — introduced 13 new boundary wire-free models for the 2025 season, bringing its wire-free lineup to 24 models and pushing Gardena wire-free units into big-box retail for the first time.

2. Supply Chain Scale and Falling Prices

Chinese manufacturers have compressed product cycles and costs. Industry analysis from Huaxi Securities estimates navigation and obstacle-avoidance systems account for about 60% of the cost of a mid-to-high-end RTK-plus-vision unit — the exact component layer where scale drives the fastest price declines.

The competitive field now splits into three camps: power tool and garden incumbents (Husqvarna, Chervon, Positec/Worx), robotics-native brands (Segway Navimow, Ecovacs, Dreame), and venture-backed specialists (Mammotion, Lymow, TerraMow, and others).

3. Regulation Against Small Gas Engines

California’s AB 1346 directed regulators to end sales of new small off-road gas engines, including lawn mowers, and the rule took effect January 1, 2024. The state has more than 16.7 million such engines — more than its passenger cars.

Existing equipment can still be used, so the impact is gradual. But every gas mower that reaches end of life in a regulated market becomes a battery-powered replacement decision — and robotic models are one of the most compelling options in that decision set.

4. Labor Scarcity in Commercial Grounds Care

Landscaping companies face persistent crew shortages and rising wages. Autonomous mowers let one technician supervise multiple machines, shifting labor from mowing to higher-margin services like trimming, enhancements, and irrigation.

Husqvarna reports double-digit annual growth in its professional robotic segment every year since launching its CEORA platform in 2021. For a closer look at operator economics, see our guide to calculating break-even for commercial robot mowers.

5. Attractive Unit Economics

Robotic mowers carry structurally better margins than legacy outdoor power equipment. Ninebot’s robotics segment, heavily driven by mower sales, reported gross margins of 53% in 2023, 56% in H1 2024, and 51% in 2024, compared with roughly 30% for leading traditional OPE brands.

Those margins are attracting capital and new entrants — which means they will compress. Plan for margin erosion of several points as competition intensifies, and look to software, accessories, and services to defend profitability.

The Headwinds Executives Must Plan Around

Price anchoring. Basic push mowers sell for under $100; capable robotic models typically start above $1,000. Total-cost-of-ownership messaging is mandatory, not optional.

Yard complexity. U.S. lawns are larger, more sloped, and more tree-covered than typical European gardens, with thicker warm-season grasses that demand more cutting power.

Service gaps. A high-ticket outdoor robot needs local setup, warranty repair, and seasonal support. Many new entrants sell online with thin or nonexistent service networks.

Trade and tariff exposure. Heavy reliance on Chinese manufacturing creates margin risk from tariffs and trade policy shifts. Several brands are diversifying production into Southeast Asia in response.

Theft and security. Expensive machines operating unattended in front yards need anti-theft features, GPS tracking, and insurance-friendly documentation.

Most category leaders now run a hybrid. Retail partnerships are accelerating: Lowe’s has partnered with Chinese brands including Segway Navimow and Sunseeker, putting wire-free robots in front of mainstream U.S. shoppers. Meanwhile, rental and subscription models are lowering the entry barrier for commercial operators, as we covered in why commercial landscapers are renting robotic mowers.

A Five-Step Growth Playbook for Robot Mower Executives

Understanding the market is only half the job. Use this framework to turn industry data into an actionable growth plan.

Step 1: Build a Bottom-Up Market Model

Replace top-down research figures with your own model. It is more defensible with investors and more useful for planning.

Count lawn-owning households in your target region.

Filter for “robot-suitable” lawns by size, slope, and terrain your products can handle.

Apply a realistic penetration curve (current rate → 5-year target).

Add replacement demand based on expected product lifespan.

Multiply by your ASP and your target share.

Formula: Annual Revenue Opportunity

(Suitable lawns × annual penetration gain) + (Installed base ÷ product lifespan in years) × ASP × target share

Step 2: Match Navigation Technology to Regional Terrain

A product optimized for a 500-square-meter German garden will struggle on a wooded half-acre in Virginia. Segment your lineup by terrain profile, not just lawn size.

Prioritize RTK-plus-vision or LiDAR fusion for tree-heavy North American markets.

Invest in all-wheel drive and slope handling for hilly regions.

Validate cutting performance on warm-season grasses like Bermuda, zoysia, and St. Augustine.

Step 3: Engineer the Out-of-Box Experience

Setup is where most negative reviews originate. Measure and minimize “time to first successful mow.”

Target under 60 minutes from unboxing to first full cut.

Offer guided mapping and remote setup assistance in the app.

Provide a paid local installation option through dealers or service partners.

Step 4: Build Service Density Before Sales Density

In high-ticket outdoor robotics, service coverage drives repeat purchases and referrals. Map authorized repair coverage before launching paid acquisition in a metro.

Recruit existing outdoor power equipment dealers as service partners.

Stock spare blades, wheels, and batteries regionally.

Track first-contact resolution and repair turnaround as board-level KPIs.

Step 5: Develop a Commercial and Recurring Revenue Arm

Consumer hardware sales are seasonal and margin-compressing. Commercial fleets, subscriptions, and service plans smooth revenue and raise lifetime value.

Launch a fleet program for landscapers, HOAs, schools, and sports facilities.

Bundle extended warranties, blade subscriptions, and premium app features.

Publish operator ROI data — such as our analysis of commercial robotic mowers vs. traditional equipment — to shorten sales cycles.

Real-World Scenario: A Mid-Size Brand Enters the U.S. Southeast

To ground the framework, consider a hypothetical brand — “Brand X” — with a strong European business and a new RTK-plus-vision lineup. It is deciding whether to launch in the U.S. Southeast. All figures below are illustrative assumptions, not market data.

The Bottom-Up Model

Target households: 6 million lawn-owning households across selected metros.

Robot-suitable share: 40%, or 2.4 million lawns.

Penetration gain: From 2% to 6% over four years — about 24,000 new adopters per year.

ASP and share: $1,600 ASP and a 15% share target yields roughly $5.8 million in annual new-unit revenue by year four, before replacement demand and services.

The Decisions That Follow

That revenue opportunity does not justify a nationwide dealer build-out. It does justify a focused launch: two metros, a partnership with 15–20 existing outdoor power equipment dealers for setup and repair, and an Amazon listing to capture search demand.

Brand X also validates performance on Bermuda and zoysia in a pre-launch field program — the kind of structured evaluation offered through our robot mower beta testing and product evaluation program — and adds a landscaper fleet pilot to test commercial demand without heavy upfront investment.

What to Watch: Industry Indicators for 2027

North American penetration crossing 5% — the likely inflection point for mainstream adoption.

Entry-level wire-free pricing below $800, which would dramatically widen the addressable market.

Base-station-free RTK via cloud or network correction, following Husqvarna’s cloud approach.

Consolidation as smaller hardware startups struggle to fund service networks.

Multi-function yard robots that combine mowing with snow clearing, leaf collection, or trimming.

Frequently Asked Questions

How fast is the robot lawn mower industry growing?

Published forecasts range from about 7.5% to 22% compound annual growth, depending on methodology. Unit data points higher in the near term: global robotic mower sales reportedly more than quadrupled year over year in the first half of 2025.

Which region leads robotic mower adoption?

Europe leads, holding roughly 42% of global market value in 2025 according to Fortune Business Insights, with the Nordic countries showing the highest household penetration at around 40%.

Who are the largest robot mower companies?

Global Market Insights identifies Husqvarna as the share leader at over 18% in 2025, with Husqvarna, Bosch, Worx, John Deere, and Ambrogio together holding about 54%. In the wire-free segment, Segway Navimow has claimed the top retail volume position for two consecutive years.

How to Cite This Research

Journalists, analysts, and bloggers are welcome to reference the data, tables, and figures in this article. Please credit and link to https://t.co/vIkAPzptiM, “Robot Lawn Mower Industry Growth: 2026 Market Data, Adoption Gaps, and a Growth Playbook for Executives.” We update this page as new industry data is released.

The Bottom Line

Robot lawn mower industry growth is no longer a question of whether, but of where and how fast. Wire-free navigation has removed the biggest adoption barrier, Chinese supply chains have reset cost curves, and regulation is steadily squeezing gas equipment.

The largest prize — North America — remains barely tapped. The brands that win it will be the ones that pair terrain-appropriate technology with real service infrastructure and recurring revenue models.
