The Pope never said "oligarchs."

Go read it, Senator. I did. Pope Leo XIV told artists at the Vatican there's an ontological difference between human art and what a machine spits out by statistical calculation. A difference in what each thing IS, before you even ask whether it looks nice. The human has a spark. The algorithm doesn't.

That's the whole point. That's all of it.

He didn't name a single CEO. He didn't say art was being destroyed. He didn't ask Congress for a thing. And he sure didn't say "Big Tech oligarchs."

You did. You took a Pope's reflection on the human soul and stapled your bumper sticker to the bottom of it. That's like spray-painting "TAX THE RICH" across the Sistine Chapel ceiling and telling everybody Michelangelo would've wanted it.

And here's the funniest part, Bernie. The Pope warned about something that produces content "through statistical calculation based on millions of" old examples, with no spark of its own.

Senator, have you read your own feed?

Every single post. "Oligarchs." "Billionaire class." "Pay their fair share." Thirty-five years of the same twelve words, rearranged in a slightly different order every morning. If anybody in this conversation is generating content by statistical calculation based on millions of previous posts... it's you. You're a chatbot with a Senate pin. The Pope just described you, and you quote-tweeted it like a compliment.

You're a pop-up ad that learned to talk.

Now let's go through your three sentences, because only one of them actually belongs to the Pope.

"Art is not some kind of superfluous luxury." Fine. Agreed. The Church has never treated art like a doily on a coffee table. Neither have I.

"It is a crucial part of the human experience." Also fine. Two for two. Don't get used to it.

"We cannot let Big Tech oligarchs destroy it." And there it is. Same word you used on Kimmel's set. Same word at the San Francisco rally, holding hands with Ro Khanna like two wedding-cake toppers made of hypocrisy. Same word on every post this month. The Pope talked about the soul. You turned it into the shareholder.

You're a weather balloon full of hot air, Senator. Up you go, every morning, same direction, no matter which way the wind's actually blowing.

Here's the part I can't let slide, because I teach science.

When the Pope says there's an ontological difference, he means the MACHINE has no inner life. No soul. No spark. It's a tool. That's a completely different claim from "the company that built the tool is destroying art." You mashed the two together like a kid mixing every color in the paint set and wondering why it all came out brown.

We've had this exact panic before. When the camera showed up, people swore painting was dead. When the printing press showed up, people swore it would ruin the scribes. Synthesizers were going to kill music. Photoshop was going to kill photography.

Painting survived. Music survived. And the very first major book Gutenberg printed on his "dangerous" new machine was the Bible.

The tool never had a spark. The PERSON using it always did. That's the line the Pope drew, and you erased it and drew a villain in its place.

Your argument is a cardboard cutout of a thought. Looks fine from across the room. Walk up close and there's nothing behind it.

Now. Let me tell you about the "oligarchs" who built the art you're suddenly so worried about.

Do you know who paid for the Renaissance, Bernie?

The Medici. A family of filthy-rich bankers in Florence. Lorenzo de' Medici took a teenage Michelangelo into his own household. Pope Julius II commissioned the Sistine Chapel ceiling. Rich patrons, bankers, and guilds paid for almost every masterpiece you can name from that whole era.

If you'd been running Florence in 1490 and taxed the "oligarchs" out of town, there's no David. No Sistine ceiling. No Renaissance. Just a lot of very talented guys standing around with no paint, no marble, and a pamphlet about fair shares.

Funny how a rich man paying for art is "patronage" in a museum and "oligarchy" on your X account.

And speaking of rich men. Three houses, Senator. A lake place. $221,000 on chartered private jets in one quarter of 2025. Millions in book royalties. And there you are, a millionaire, pointing at other rich people and calling them oligarchs. You're the hood ornament on a car with no engine. Shiny, loud, out front, and not actually moving anything.

As an anatomy teacher, I'll add one more thing. Michelangelo studied the human body up close to learn exactly how muscles and bones work, so his marble would look like it could breathe. That's the spark the Pope is talking about. A human being doing the hard, messy, human work of understanding how God put us together. No algorithm did that for him. And no wealth tax would have helped him do it either.

And look where you posted this, Senator.

You posted a warning about machines... on X. Through a phone. Through a cell tower. Onto servers in a data center. The same kind of data center you told us last week was "threatening humanity." The week before that, you wanted to pause AI completely.

You keep sending warnings about the machine THROUGH the machine. You're a wind chime in a hurricane, Bernie. Lots of noise. Zero effect on the weather.

And here's a question I mean sincerely. You're quoting the Pope like he's on your team. Do you also agree with the Catholic Church that every human life is sacred from conception? Because the Church is a lot clearer on that than it is on Big Tech.

Or do you only agree with the Pope when he fits on a campaign flyer?

That's called cherry-picking, Senator. Grabbing the one line you like out of a two-thousand-year tradition and ignoring everything around it. It's like reading one verse and building a whole sermon on it without checking the verses on either side. I spend a lot of time on the context of scripture. You might try it with the Pope.

So here's some context, since we're talking about God and art.

In Genesis 1, God creates. Then He makes mankind in His own image. One of the most human things about us is that we MAKE things, because our Creator does.

And in Exodus 31, when God wanted the tabernacle built, He didn't form a committee or pass a tax. He called a craftsman named Bezalel and filled him with His Spirit, with wisdom, understanding, and skill in every kind of craftsmanship. In the Bible, artistic talent is a gift from God, given to a PERSON.

Not to a government. Not to a machine. And not to a senator who wants to tax the patrons.

That's Quinn's Law Number Two, Bernie: if you want to know what liberals are up to, watch what they accuse conservatives of doing. You accuse Big Tech of destroying human art, while you use Big Tech to bend a Pope's words into a fundraising slogan, written in the same recycled phrases you've been generating since 1991.

You're the mall Santa of socialism, Senator. Same suit every year, same promises, and the presents never actually show up.

You're a garage sale of recycled slogans, and every item is marked "free."

And honestly, you've got all the creative spark of a lava lamp. Lots of slow motion. Nothing actually gets made.

So here's my offer. Leave the theology to the theologians, the art to the artists, and the money to the people who earned it. If you really want to protect human creativity, stop trying to tax the people who've been paying artists since before the printing press.

But what do I know? I'm only an anatomy teacher who knows why Michelangelo studied the human body, a Christian who reads scripture in context, and a guy who noticed the only thing in this conversation running on statistical calculation is Bernie's X account.

Friedrich Merz arrived in Kiev carrying a formula Berlin has been circulating since May. Full accession in the coming years is treated in European capitals as unrealistic. What he put on the table instead was an invented halfway house: “associate membership,” a seat in the room, a look at the single market, observer status in the European Council, the Commission and the Parliament, and no vote. 

 Zelensky refused it on the spot. He wants a chair with a ballot, not a folding stool by the wall. Politico called the membership question one of the sharpest points of friction between the two men. That friction is the story. The rest is costume.

An associate badge is not a treaty. It does not bind 27 capitals to a date, a budget line or a veto waiver. Hungary, and others who have already slowed the file, would still hold the brake. Merz can talk of acceleration in a press conference and still hand Kiev a status that does not exist in the treaties. Zelensky read the offer as half a membership and said so. 

The demand for “full and equal” standing collided with a chancellor who will not spend political capital to deliver it.

A WAITING ROOM WITH A VIEW

Observer status sounds generous until the agenda is read. Trade access can be priced, limited and reversed. A commissioner without a portfolio does not write law. Deputies without a vote do not move a directive. Meetings can be attended and then ignored. 

 For a government that has spent four years selling Europe the idea that the Union’s future runs through Kiev, a non-voting gallery seat is a public demotion. Merz floated the same design in a May letter to António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen, framing it as a bridge while reforms continue. Kiev answered then, and answered again in the capital: no bridge that ends short of the chamber.

The enlargement method was built for slow candidates, not for a state at war that wants the flag on the building by 2027. Agriculture, rule of law, minority rights and budget shares are not slogans. They are chapters. Germany’s own industry has no appetite for an overnight competitor inside the customs union with a full vote on industrial policy. Merz governs that industry’s country. His caution in Kyiv tracked the interest, not the poster.

THE COLLAPSE AT HOME

The same week, German polling described a chancellor the public has already written off. In the ARD-Deutschlandtrend taken at the end of September, 10 percent were satisfied with his work and 88 percent were not. That is the weakest reading for any chancellor since the series began in 1997. 

A Forsa reading for RTL/ntv put satisfaction at 11 percent. ZDF’s Politbarometer had 79 percent calling the job poor. Even a milder INSA weekend figure, 28 percent satisfied and 62 percent dissatisfied, still leaves him underwater. 

Union support in the Sunday questions sits around a fifth of the vote. 

The AfD is ahead in several of those same surveys.

A leader with those numbers does not export a national crusade. He manages a coalition that the country has stopped believing. Satisfaction this low is not a quarrel inside one party. It is a refusal of the governing project: energy bills, industrial stagnation, migration, and a foreign line that keeps asking households to underwrite a war they did not vote to enter. 

When nine in ten respondents withhold approval, Berlin cannot honestly claim that “Germany” is mobilized against Moscow. The chancellery is. The electorate is busy withdrawing the mandate.

NOT A VERDICT AGAINST RUSSIA

Low ratings are not a friendship treaty, and nobody should pretend a poll is a foreign policy. They do kill the slogan that the Federal Republic stands as one against Russia. 

 A chancellor at historic disapproval cannot launder his Kiev script as the people’s will. Voters who have already abandoned the Union for the AfD, or who simply sit in the dissatisfied column, are not signing up for accelerated accession, open-ended budget transfers or a security clause smuggled in through a political letter. Merz’s own offer in Kiev — market access and a silent chair — already conceded that full membership is not coming on Zelensky’s clock. The German street has conceded something colder: it is done underwriting the performance.

Europe’s treasury mood points the same way. Fresh cash to plug Kyiv’s budget hole is no longer waved through as an act of identity. Packages get sliced, conditioned on reforms, and argued over. A state that cannot pass a domestic confidence test will not volunteer a blank cheque abroad. 

 That is arithmetic, not romance.

WHAT THE MEETING ACTUALLY SETTLED

Kiev wanted a shortcut into the Union. Berlin offered a laminated visitor pass and kept the vote. Zelenskyy rejected the pass. Merz flew home to a country that rates him at the bottom of the modern chancellor table, with his bloc trailing or tied with a party that has made distance from this war part of its pitch. 

 The collision is not a diplomatic mishap. It is the moment the accession story stopped being a promise and became a quarrel between a supplicant who will accept only equality and a chancellor who no longer has the public behind him to grant it.

Former New Jersey Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell has resigned after an independent investigation found that he sexually harassed a staff member and repeatedly violated state ethics rules. Governor Mikie Sherrill accepted his resignation on September 25 after publicly calling for him to step down. (https://t.co/QuFFdM3qVG)

The investigation found what Sherrill described as “serious, repeated violations of state policy,” including a substantiated finding of sexual harassment. Caldwell has continued to argue that the report was flawed and said he resigned because he did not want the controversy to distract from the Sherrill administration. His attorney has also said they are exploring legal options to challenge the findings and create what they describe as a fairer record. (News 12 - Default)

The episode highlights a growing problem around the use of AI in public disputes. Large language models can summarize documents and identify arguments, but their outputs depend heavily on the prompts, context, and material they are given. They do not independently determine guilt, innocence, or legal responsibility.

text:
Dracaena Malfoy felt as if she had died in the forest. She had watched as that insufferable Potter had walked right towards his death. She had stood there, letting her parents hold her back, letting her fears hold her back. Proving once and for all that everyone in the Wizarding World was right: Dracaena Malfoy was unworthy of the Love that had been offered to her by the heroic, magnanimous, idiotic Harry Potter.

She barely noticed that the procession, led by the
Dark Lord and the quietly sobbing Hagrid, had stopped. It was not until her mother's hands on her shoulders gripped tight and pulled her to a stop near the front that she realized with a jolt that the Dark Lord had led them to the courtyard of Hogwarts, where every single one of the rebellious Wizards and Witches within would be able to see the broken corpse of the lanky, stupid, brave Wizard in Hagrid's arms.

She watched the Dark Lord pass close by Harry, his snake-like face sneering down at the body of the only one who could have defeated him. He raised his wand, and a moment later his voice magically magnified so that it swelled through the grounds.

“Harry Potter is dead. He was killed as he ran away, trying to save himself while you lay down your lives for him. We bring you his body as proof that your hero is gone.”

Dracaena tensed at that. A lie. A lie? Everyone knew that only Harry could defeat the Dark Lord. So why would he lie? Ease? Yes. Her mother's grounding grip on her shoulders reminded her of that much. He had already defeated the rebels; it was only a question of how many of his own followers had to shed blood in order to make it known permanently in the bones of the defeated. She shrank into herself; passive, choiceless, and utterly undeserving of looking even at the corpse of the boy she had... she refused to finish the thought. It hurt far too much.

The Dark Lord continued speaking,“The battle is won.
You have lost half of your fighters.  My Death Eaters outnumber you, and the Boy Who  Lived is finished. There must be no more war. Anyone  who continues to resist, man, woman, or child, will be  slaughtered, as will every member of their family.  Come out of the castle now, kneel before me, and you  shall be spared. Your parents and children, your brothers and sisters will live and be forgiven, and you  will join me in the new world we shall build together.” 

There was silence in the grounds and from the castle. Dracaena did not dare look up at any of them, to see the agony of Harry's death in their eyes. The disappointment with her, as ever, being nothing but one who could never do anything but watch and obey, even when Harry Potter himself had told them that she was more. She clenched her fists at her sides. Her ultimate legacy: proving Harry Potter was an idiot.

In First Year she probably would have found that funny. In First Year. 

“Come,” said the Dark Lord. His voice demanded eyes, and Dracaena watched as Hagrid was forced to follow. The Dark Lord strode in front of him, wearing the great snake  Nagini around his shoulders, now free of her enchanted cage.

“Follow, Dracy,” her father urged quietly, his voice the only thing that forced her leaden feet to stumble forward on the cobblestone after the Dark Lord.

“Harry,” sobbed Hagrid. “Oh, Harry... Harry ...” 

Dracaena heard the sobs of the half giant and felt as if they were echoes of some deep part of her that she was desperately trying to not let out. She did not deserve to mourn him, after all. She had not defended him when no one else was there to even try. She... had not loved him enough.

“Stop.” 

The Death Eaters came to a halt in a large semicircle behind their Lord in the courtyard of the school. Bellatrix, with her ever present mad cruelty, had ensured that Lucius could not take his family to the edges. They were forced to remain directly near the Dark Lord as the doors of the Entrance Hall were pulled open. Any moment, the people that Harry had died to protect would see him. And they would see her. A Death Eater. The greatest traitor to the Boy who Lived.

“You chose well,” Bellatrix whispered to Dracaena in the moment of silence, as if her public refusal to stand with a boy everyone had known she cared for had redeemed the failures of the Malfoy family in the eyes of the Death Eaters. Dracaena should have felt relieved. It meant her family would survive. Instead she felt a violent urge to vomit.

“NO!” 

The scream was a blessing to Dracaena, for it acted as
a distraction from her disgust with her own weakness.
She had never expected or dreamed that Professor McGonagall could make such a sound, though. Her only memories of the woman were of a stern face and spells cast in the heat of battle against Death Eaters this year and the prior year.

She flinched when she heard another woman laughing at her side, and saw Bellatrix was nearly taking pleasure in McGonagall’s despair.

Dracaena felt the urge to vomit return, and instead looked
towards the open doorway filling with people, as the survivors of the battle came out onto the front steps to face their vanquishers and see the truth of Harry’s death for themselves. The Dark Lord took an inhumanly smooth step to the side to make sure everyone could see the dead body. He began stroking Nagini’s head with a single white finger. He seemed to be bathing in the agonized despair of those present like it was a good wine.

“No!” 

“Harry! HARRY!”

Weasley's and Granger's voices were worse  than McGonagall’s; McGonagall's agony had been that of a mentor. Perhaps a grandmother, in some respect. But the screams of Harry's friends were like those of Hagrid; they felt
as if they had been torn from Dracaena's own heart. Yet she
forced herself to stand silent even as their gazes turned on her. She made herself see the disappointment. The hate. And... ah. Betrayal. Harry's word had been enough for them to think of her...
perhaps not as a friend, but as one who could become a friend. And now even that had been killed in the cradle.

The pair's cries acted like a trigger; the crowd of survivors took up the cause, screaming and yelling abuse at the Death Eaters, and even more directly at Dracaena herself. Mentions of her dance with Harry at the Yule Ball that now felt like a lifetime ago were common. His mother had died for him and you could not even speak for him. The focus on her seemed to draw some level of ire from the Dark Lord. 

“SILENCE!” he cried, and there was a bang and a flash of bright light, and silence was forced upon them all. “It is over! Set him down, Hagrid, at my feet, where he belongs!” 

Dracaena watched the lanky, messy haired idiot be lowered to the grass. Hagrid, despite his size, was gentle. As if he was gently placing an infant upon the front step of a home so many years ago. 

“You see?” said the Dark Lord as he paced theatrically in front of Harry's corpse. “Harry Potter is dead! Even the woman he claimed to love stands among my ranks. Do you understand now, deluded ones? He was nothing, ever, but a boy who  relied on others to sacrifice themselves for him!” 

“He beat you!” yelled Weasley, and the charm broke, and the defenders of Hogwarts were shouting and screaming again until a second, more powerful bang extinguished their voices once more. 

“He was killed while trying to sneak out of the castle grounds,” said Voldemort, and there was relish in his voice for the lie, “killed while trying to save himself — ” 

But he broke off. Longbottom was charging through the line of and had cast a hex right at the Dark Lord himself as if it had been the simplest thing. Dracaena felt her stomach lurch once more. It was that easy? How was it that easy to try, even knowing you would fail? The Dark Lord did not even bother looking as he deflected the spell and cast his own to bring Longbottom to his knees. A wave of his wand and Longbottom's wand was sent skittering across the stone while the Dark Lord laughed.

“And who is this?” he said in his soft snake’s hiss. “Who has volunteered to demonstrate what happens to those who continue to fight when the battle is lost?” 

Bellatrix gave a delighted laugh. 

“It is Neville Longbottom, my Lord! The boy who has been giving the Carrows so much trouble! The son of the Aurors, remember?” 

“Ah, yes, I remember,” said the Dark Lord, looking down at Neville, who was struggling back to his feet,  unarmed and unprotected, standing in the no-man’s- land between the survivors and the Death Eaters. 

“But you are a pureblood, aren’t you, my brave boy?” the Dark Lord asked Longbottom, who stood facing him, his empty hands curled in fists. 

“So what if I am?” said Longbottom loudly.

Dracaena hated Longbottom in that moment. Not for any rational reason. Envy. He was standing up for Harry's memory. Against the absurd lie that the Dark Lord was spinning that Harry was a coward.
That he had abandoned those he loved. That he was anything like the
girl he had claimed to love that now stood among the ranks of the
Death Eaters.

“You show spirit and bravery, and you come of noble stock. You will make a very valuable Death Eater. We need your kind, Neville Longbottom.” 

“I’ll join you when hell freezes over,” said Neville. Dracaena noted with a start she had just called him Neville in her mind. “Dumbledore’s Army!” he shouted, and there was an answering cheer from the crowd, whom the Dark Lord's Silencing Charms seemed unable to hold. 

“Very well,” said the Dark Lord, and Dracaena heard in his voice a danger that even a Cruciatus Curse could not replicate fully. “If that is your choice, Longbottom, we revert to the original plan. On your head,” he said quietly, “be it.” 

The Dark Lord waved his wand. Seconds later, out of one of the castle’s shattered windows, something that looked like a misshapen bird flew through the half light and landed in his outstretched claw. He shook the mildewed  object by its pointed end and it dangled, empty and ragged: the Sorting Hat. 

“There will be no more Sorting at Hogwarts School,” said the Dark Lord. “There will be no more Houses. The emblem, shield, and colors of my noble ancestor,  Salazar Slytherin, will suffice for everyone. Won’t they, Neville Longbottom?”

He pointed his wand at Neville, who grew rigid and 
still and walked a half step forward. Then... he stopped and smiled like a snake preparing to bite. “No... Dracaena.” He turned and the horrible weight of his gaze was suddenly squarely on her. Just another chance to twist the knife by showing that the woman Harry had loved was wholeheartedly on his side.

She felt a surge of anger. Had she not done enough for him!? She had betrayed the man she loved with her fear! She had failed to be the woman he claimed she was deep down! She... Her indignation deflated into self loathing. What else could she do? Her path had been chosen. Refusal would kill her parents. And then what would all of this have even been for? She felt her parents hesitate themselves. But, slowly, they let her go.

She moved forward with a grace that had been drilled into her in years of etiquette classes as a young girl. 'A Malfoy never stumbles, Dracaena. And you are the consummate Malfoy,' her father had once told her. She stopped and bowed her head in front of the Dark Lord, who placed the hat in her hand like it was a weapon. “Place it upon the Blood Traitor, my dear,” he hissed triumphantly above her.

“Y-Yes, my lord,” she whispered. The Girl who Betrayed the Boy who Lived held the hat in both hands and turned to Neville. Brave Neville. Far braver than her. She remembered suddenly when she had  taken his Remembrall in First Year. A stupid memory. Except... looking back, that was when it had started, wasn't it? A girlish crush on the one boy who had told her no. Who had refused to do the wrong thing even if it was going to cost him the one place in the entire world he finally felt at home. Knowing now what she knew about the Dursleys, he had essentially risked the only happiness he could have to do what was right. And he had been rewarded for it, infuriating her and impressing her and... And making her want to be like him, deep down.

She stopped for a moment a few feet from the Dark Lord.

“Well?” his silky voice was becoming impatient. Angry. The hat was heavy in her hands. She held it sideways in her and ran her fingers along the inner brim. It had not even touched her skull before it had screamed 'Slytherin!'  to the Great Hall. She was where Slytherins belonged. With the Heir of Salazar Slytherin. With the Dark...

With...

“Dracy, go...” Lucius Malfoy urged, voice terrified for the first time in a long time not for himself, but for the young woman he had raised.

“Voldemort.” The courtyard went silent when someone said that word. Who? Dracaena saw all eyes on her and realized, somehow, that it had been her voice! She looked down at the hat and swore almost that she could see... red and silver within. Impossible. No. Harry had told her the story about the Chamber. About the Sword only a True Gryffindor could pull from the hat. Only someone who had decided upon bravery and self sacrifice and... and all the infuriatingly 'Harry Potter' behaviors that would end with one dying on the ground. She turned around and took a shuddering breath. “Voldemort.” Not 'Dark Lord' not 'my Lord' not even 'Lord Voldemort,' as his position demanded. “No.”

“Bloody Hell...” Weasley muttered, his whisper breaking the silence charm again.

But no else one said anything, as if afraid it would shatter the odd, impossible charm of seeing Malfoy, cruel and capricious and demanding and born to be a Death Eater say 'No' to Voldemort when every Death Eater was watching and his Snake was looking right at her.

“Dracaena -!” Lucius snapped, only to freeze as Voldemort's hand came up to silence him.

“No?” Voldemort seemed caught between amusement and a pure, blinding, hateful rage. But his self control won out. “I would hope this is a poorly timed joke, Dracaena.”

An out. She should take it. She should. Any Slytherin would take that out so they could survive, so – Her eyes flicked to Harry's body. And in that moment, she felt decidedly unlike a Slytherin. Or, rather, she was perhaps what a Slytherin should have been. Cunning and Ambition and Leadership were the marks of a Slytherin. Following a Dark Lord who had been afraid of an infant? It was unbecoming of any who bore the name of Salazar Slytherin upon their robes! And... and it would be an insult to the man who had been perhaps the most Gryffindor boy to ever live since the man himself. “No.” The hat felt even heavier now. She felt her fingers curl around cool, dangerous metal within the hat.

“No...” Voldemort sighed and turned to his Death Eaters. “Very well.” He raised his wand right at Narcissa Malfoy. Lucius' eyes went wide and he tried to pull his wife behind him.

“NO!” Dracaena shrieked. But she did not pull back from her decision. The die had been cast and, despite the agony that would soon come, it offered a sort of... clarity. No matter what she did now, Voldemort would not change his course. And so, neither would she. Not in this moment that was far too important to her.

Bellatrix was clapping. Clapping! At the impending death of her own family! Voldemort's voice rose with a cruel joy as he prepared to snuff out one of the twenty eight pureblood families he claimed to champion. “Avada -!”

And then many things happened at the same
moment. 

They heard uproar from the distant boundary of the 
school as what sounded like hundreds of people came 
swarming over the out-of-sight walls and pelted 
toward the castle, uttering loud war cries. At the 
same time, Grawp came lumbering around the side of 
the castle and yelled, “HAGGER!” His cry was answered by roars from Voldemort’s giants: They ran  at Grawp like bull elephants, making the earth quake.  Then came hooves and the twangs of bows, and 
arrows were suddenly falling amongst the Death 
Eaters, who broke ranks, shouting their surprise. 
A moment of distraction.

In one swift, fluid motion that only a noblewoman could truly unleash, Dracaena pulled her hand from within the hat and drew drew from its depths something that only a True Gryffindorcould ever pull from within the hat's brim. 

The slash of the silver blade could not be heard over 
the roar of the oncoming crowd or the sounds of the 
clashing giants or of the stampeding centaurs, and 
yet it seemed to draw every eye. With a single stroke 
Dracaena  Malfoy – Slytherin, traitor twice over, and the unworthy Girl who Loved the Boy who Lived - sliced off the great snake’s head, which spun high into the air, gleaming in the light flooding from the entrance hall.

Voldemort’s mouth opened in a scream of fury that nobody could hear, but that Dracaena could feel in the marrow of her bones. Her heart was pounding in her chest and even as Voldemort raised his wand towards her when the  snake’s body thudded to the ground at his feet, she could not find it in herself to regret this decision. She was going to die. Her parents, likely, would also pay the price. She did regret that, perhaps. But for the first time, she felt as if Dracaena Malfoy was worthy of the look in Harry's eyes when he had seen her at the Yule Ball. When he had argued with his own friends that she was worthy of being among them. She felt... free.

And then the curse that Voldemort cast bounced off of a shield charm that had appeared between them from nothing. Battle began. Screams, spells... War, returned to Hogwarts. But there was only one thing that her ears noticed. “HARRY!” Hagrid shouted. “HARRY — WHERE’S HARRY?” Her eyes flicked to the ground. Gone. His corpse was gone– no... no, not his corpse. Harry. Harry!

And surrounded by the most dangerous and cruel wizards in the world hurling curses, Dracaena could only look up at the sky and laugh. Even when Neville grabbed her and dragged her back, she kept laughing – crying, maybe. “He's alive!” she sobbed. All was right in the world. She'd been rewarded for doing the right thing? Her? “Potter, you... you idiot!”
“Bloody hell, Malfoy, get it together!” Weasley snapped as he helped Neville drag her back inside the great hall of the castle. She just kept laughing the whole way in like a madwoman.

text:
There is a reason the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna has always begun with the young. Not because the JVP loves youth, but because the young, with their idealism, their hunger for justice, their impatience with the world as it is, and their incomplete understanding of the world as it works, are the most valuable raw material for any movement that seeks to replace thinking with obedience, questioning with loyalty, and individual judgement with collective submission. For over five decades, the JVP has systematically targeted Sri Lanka's young people in schools, universities, and villages, not to educate them, but to conscript them intellectually: to narrow their world to a single ideology, to close the doors of their minds, and to convince them that the party's truth is the only truth. The result is not an empowered generation. It is a generation that has been taught what to think rather than how to think, and that difference has cost Sri Lanka more than any economic crisis, war, or natural disaster.

It began with Rohana Wijeweera in the late 1960s. The JVP's founder developed a programme of political indoctrination called the "Five Lectures", a structured curriculum delivered to young recruits in secret locations, often in cemeteries, remote coastal areas, and hidden "education camps." The five lectures covered the economic crisis, neo-colonialism, Indian expansionism, the failure of Sri Lanka's existing left parties, and the necessity of violent revolution. They were designed, within Wijeweera's own framework, to explain "in simple and plain language the politics of social revolution."

Yet they were not education; they were programming. The lectures presented a closed ideological system, a world divided into oppressors and the oppressed, exploiters and the exploited, enemies of the revolution and soldiers of the revolution, with no room for nuance, complexity, or dissent. A young person who completed the Five Lectures emerged not with a broader understanding of economics, politics, or history, but with a narrower one: a world reduced to Marxist-Leninist categories, a conviction that violence was the only path to change, and an allegiance to the party that superseded all others, including family, community, and independent thought.

Those who completed all five lectures and volunteered for combat, approximately 9,000 recruits, received military training. They were not students becoming revolutionaries; they were children becoming soldiers. The political indoctrination classes, as historians have documented, "reinforced the youths' anxieties and persuaded them to embark on the path of violence."

The result was the 1971 insurrection, in which an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 young people, most of them barely out of school, lost their lives. They died not for a cause they had independently evaluated and freely chosen, but for one that had been installed in their minds through a systematic programme of ideological conditioning conducted by adults who sent youth to attack police stations while remaining in hiding themselves.

The second insurrection was worse. Between 1987 and 1989, the JVP, again operating through youth recruited in schools and universities, conducted a campaign of assassinations, beheadings, and terror that killed an estimated 60,000 people. Young men and women radicalised through JVP cells were used as instruments of political murder: killing political opponents, trade unionists, bus drivers who refused to join strikes, workers who defied JVP-called hartals, and ordinary citizens deemed enemies of the revolution.

These were not hardened militants. They were students, school-leavers, and unemployed rural youth who had been psychologically conditioned to believe that killing in the name of the revolution was not murder, but duty. The JVP's method was the same as that of every totalitarian movement in history: recruit young people whose minds are still forming, isolate them from competing ideas, immerse them in a closed ideological framework, provide the purpose and belonging their circumstances had denied them, and then direct them toward violence. The youth were the ammunition; the party leadership was the gun.

When the insurrection was crushed with terrible brutality by a state that matched the JVP's violence with its own, the leadership that had dispatched those young people to kill and die was gone. Wijeweera was captured and extrajudicially executed, and the party was banned. Tens of thousands of families, the families of the young people who had been recruited, indoctrinated, and destroyed, were left with nothing but grief and the knowledge that their children had been consumed by the very revolution that used them.

The JVP's capture of Sri Lanka's university system is perhaps its most enduring and destructive legacy, one that continues to damage young lives today.

Through the Inter University Students' Federation (IUSF), which functioned for decades as the JVP's campus arm before splintering toward the Frontline Socialist Party, the JVP established a system of political control over state universities that operates primarily through one mechanism: ragging.

Ragging, the systematic physical, psychological, and sexual harassment of incoming university students by seniors, is not a traditional Sri Lankan cultural practice. It is a political instrument. It is the mechanism through which the dominant student union asserts authority over each incoming class, identifies prospective recruits, breaks the will of those who might resist, and enforces a culture of obedience and hierarchy that mirrors the party structure outside the university gates.

The statistics are devastating. Research published in peer-reviewed journals indicates that 59 percent of Sri Lankan university students have experienced at least one form of ragging: verbal ragging affected 51 percent; psychological ragging, 34 percent; physical ragging, 24 percent; and sexual ragging, 17 percent. Fifty-four percent reported adverse health consequences. Approximately 2,000 students drop out of university annually as a direct result of ragging, and several have died by suicide.

Since the 1970s, at least seven student deaths have been directly or indirectly attributed to ragging in Sri Lankan universities. The most notorious case is that of Samantha Vithanage, a third-year management student at the University of Sri Jayewardenepura who pioneered an anti-ragging campaign on campus. In 2002, a mob of approximately 200 JVP supporters armed with clubs and stones stormed a meeting room, viciously attacking Vithanage and fellow students opposing ragging. Vithanage was killed. His crime was resisting the apparatus of intimidation through which the JVP maintained political dominance over the campus.

Vithanage's murder was not an isolated incident of campus violence; it was the logical culmination of a system engineered to ensure that no student could organise independently, think critically, or challenge the dominant faction without facing physical consequences. Ragging is not mere hazing. It is political enforcement, the party's message to every incoming student: We control this space, we control your experience, and if you resist, you will be broken.

The psychological toll on young minds is profound. Students who endure ragging absorb three enduring lessons: power belongs to those who inflict pain, obedience is the price of survival, and independent thought is dangerous. These are not the principles that cultivate scientists, entrepreneurs, artists, or civic leaders. They are the conditions that produce compliant followers, individuals conditioned to submit to authority, distrust their own judgement, and seek shelter in collective conformity rather than stand by their own convictions.

The JVP's erosion of independent thinking extends beyond indoctrination and campus violence to the systematic obstruction of educational reforms that would offer young Sri Lankans alternatives beyond party control.

For decades, the JVP and its student fronts have led the opposition against the establishment of private higher-education institutions in Sri Lanka. The campaign against the South Asian Institute of Technology and Medicine (SAITM), the country's sole private medical school at the time, was driven by JVP-aligned student unions and reinforced by the party's political apparatus. The IUSF staged prolonged protests, affiliated unions orchestrated strikes, and relentless political pressure ultimately forced the government to shut the institution down.

While framed as a defence of free education, an inherently noble principle, the practical consequence was to ensure that the state university system remained the sole accessible pathway to higher education for Sri Lankan youth. That state system is precisely what the JVP dominates through student unions, ragging, the IUSF, and an entrenched culture of political conformity. Every private university, alternative pathway, or independent institution outside the JVP's sphere of influence represents a venue where students might cultivate ideas the party has not sanctioned, build associations it cannot govern, and forge identities autonomous from the movement.

The opposition to private higher education is rooted less in protecting the underprivileged than in preserving institutional control. A student attending an independent institution is not subjected to IUSF ragging, does not attend political indoctrination framed as orientation, and encounters diverse perspectives, including market economics, liberal democracy, individual rights, and global frameworks, that conflict with rigid party doctrine. The JVP relies on the state university system remaining a near-monopoly because it serves as the party's primary recruitment pipeline.

Meanwhile, state universities, often underfunded, politically captured, disrupted by recurrent strikes, and plagued by systemic ragging, graduate students who frequently struggle to meet the demands of the modern economy. A country that channels its brightest minds into a university system commandeered by political factions produces graduates who struggle to compete with peers across India, Malaysia, Singapore, or Vietnam, nations that prioritised educational diversity, academic rigor, and global relevance while Sri Lanka preserved political monopolies on campus life.

The JVP's mechanisms have adapted to modern technology, yet the operational strategy remains unchanged: dominate the information landscape, police the boundaries of political discourse, and penalise those who dissent.

Today's digital partisans, swarming social media to harass critics of the government, brand dissenters as traitors, and circulate party talking points as objective analysis, are the modern inheritors of the Five Lectures. They have not arrived at their convictions through independent inquiry, engagement with counterarguments, or rigorous appraisal of evidence. Rather, they have undergone the same recruitment pipeline: immersion in a closed ideological framework, reinforcement through collective peer pressure, and the penalisation, now digital rather than physical, of all who disagree.

A young person who questions state policy online is met not with reasoned rebuttal, but with coordinated harassment. Anyone presenting an opposing perspective is promptly labelled a traitor, a political plant, or an enemy of the people. Inquiries into shifting statistical claims, controversial legislation, vacant judicial benches, or custodial abuses are systematically suppressed rather than answered. The agitators who once carried batons down university corridors now deploy keyboards, yet their purpose is identical: to ensure no young mind deviates from the party line.

The cumulative toll of five decades of JVP influence on Sri Lanka's youth is devastating. Thousands of young lives were extinguished in two insurrections they were conditioned to wage, while thousands more were killed, imprisoned, or forcibly disappeared in the state's brutal counter-offensives. Entire generations of undergraduates endured systemic ragging that impaired their mental well-being, stifled intellectual development, and taught them that influence is asserted through coercion rather than merit and debate. Needed reforms were stalled for decades, trapping hundreds of thousands in an educational structure serving political factions rather than students. Today, a new generation is taught across digital platforms and partisan ecosystems that tribal loyalty supersedes truth, official narratives outweigh empirical evidence, and scrutinising leadership amounts to national betrayal.

This represents the movement's enduring legacy: not the economic restructuring it promises, nor the anti-corruption platforms it advertises, but the systematic erosion of independent thought among Sri Lanka's young. A movement that originated in clandestine cemetery lectures has spent half a century constraining the intellectual horizons of youth, confining them within an ideological structure that tolerates only approved answers, penalises dissent, and produces partisan foot soldiers rather than citizens equipped to build an innovative, democratic society.

Sri Lanka's greatest asset is neither its tea, its gems, nor its strategic maritime position. It is its youth, their intellect, energy, creativity, and capacity to envision a future distinct from the past. For fifty years, that resource has been exploited for political leverage and unquestioning loyalty, leaving behind restricted perspectives, enduring trauma, and the damaging premise that independent thought is a hazard rather than a civic virtue.
